title: Solving our affordability crisis will require creative solutions and a roll-up-your-sleeves approach to create housing that works for all New Yorkers and allows them to live in dynamic, diverse, and… | David Schwartz
description:
Solving our affordability crisis will require creative solutions and a roll-up-your-sleeves approach to create housing that works for all New Yorkers and allows them to live in dynamic, diverse, and desirable neighborhoods.

Slate Property Group has been selected by HPD, alongside The Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America–Greater New York, to develop the Orion at 54-42 2nd Street in Long Island City's Hunter's Point South. Nearly 1,000 homes across three buildings, two-thirds of them permanently affordable, with 149 units of supportive housing for formerly homeless New Yorkers.

The Orion checks all those boxes and more: it will deliver nearly a thousand new homes for New Yorkers across the income spectrum and provide essential supportive services to those who need it most, all while making Long Island City more resilient to climate change. It is exactly what New York needs, and we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.

This is the first deployment of HPD's Mixed Income Market Initiative, a framework that uses market-rate units to help finance deeper affordability rather than treating the two as competing goals. Two-thirds of a building affordable is not a typical ratio, and getting there took real structuring work between the city and this development team.

The site will also house a daycare center, workforce development space, and an indoor pool operated by Commonpoint Queens and open to the surrounding community, not just residents.

Grateful to build this one alongside Volunteers of America–Greater New York and The Hudson Companies, with HPD leading the way.

title: The Grid as Platform Infrastructure: Why Underinvestment is the Real Affordability Crisis
description: As electricity prices have risen in recent months, the political response has been to demand near-term rate relief, pushing regulators and utilities to minimize costs today. But that approach inaccurately treats the grid like a commodity to be priced efficiently for today’s static demand. A near-term affordability focus risks compounding a decades-long deficit in transmission investment and firm generation, produced by fragmented planning authority, unresolved cost-allocation disputes, permitting and siting dysfunction, and utility incentives that reward small, local build-outs over large interregional lines. DOE's 2026 National Transmission Needs Study draft confirms just how narrow the grid buildout has been: interregional transmission, which delivers the highest value of any investment, accounted for less than 2% of all transmission capital spending nationally between 2016 and 2024. An electricity strategy focused only on minimizing costs today does not fix that deficit, and could result in higher costs and a less reliable grid within the decade.

🗣️ NEW REPORT: The affordability crisis has a new face: it's the insured. Turns out 'covered' and 'affordable' aren't synonyms. 30,000 people told us so.

The affordability crisis is no longer… | Natalie Davis
description:
🗣️ NEW REPORT: The affordability crisis has a new face: it's the insured. Turns out 'covered' and 'affordable' aren't synonyms. 30,000 people told us so.

The affordability crisis is no longer something that happens only to people who have been left out of the system. It is happening to people in it.

Every day, people across this country are playing by the rules — getting insured, paying premiums, choosing a doctor in their network — and still finding themselves unable to afford the care they need. They wind up with a hospital bill that bears no resemblance to what they were quoted. Calls from a debt collection agency about a doctor's appointment their plan didn't cover. A prescription they stop filling because something else had to give.

And what we hear over and over is this: 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬.

Through our work at United States of Care, we've spent years listening to more than 30,000 people across all 50 states. Our latest Pulse Check puts that reality front and center.

Here's some of what we found:
→ 21% of insured adults carry medical debt — nearly the same rate as the uninsured
 → 94% of people say hospital prices are high, and most never see them coming
 → 25% of people struggle with prescription costs, across every coverage type
 → 1 in 4 adults skip seeing their primary care provider because they can't afford it

People aren't asking for anything unreasonable. They want hospital prices that match what they were quoted. Premiums that don't double in a year. A primary care visit they can schedule without doing the math first. That's not too much to ask.

This is what a human-first look at the affordability crisis actually shows: it's not a coverage problem alone. It's a system that's failing people who are doing everything right.
